title: AIDA
subtitle: AI-Driven Distributed Autonomy
summary: An FWF project on learning-based, distributed decision-making for autonomous vehicles, building on our small-scale RoboRacer cars.
body: Autonomous vehicles that share a road need models of their own dynamics and must coordinate with other vehicles. AIDA studies how learning can support both.

The FWF record lists vehicle dynamics, large language models, recurrent neural networks, distributed multi-agent systems and federated learning as the project's topics. The project is led by Agnes Poks at TU Wien, with Daniela Rus (MIT) as international participant. The plan runs from November 2026 to April 2029 under grant PAT3743226.
The work builds on our small-scale RoboRacer experiments and vehicle-dynamics models.

title: ADEX
subtitle: Autonomous-Driving Examiner
summary: An FFG project (2020 to 2024) on training and testing autonomous driving agents with generated scenarios and formal specifications.
body: Autonomous driving agents must be trained and tested on many traffic scenarios, and their behavior must meet requirements on safety, goals and comfort. Writing these scenarios and reward signals by hand is slow.

ADEX was funded by the FFG (project 880811) and led by Radu Grosu at TU Wien. Its outputs include MATS-Gym, which generates multi-agent traffic scenarios in the CARLA simulator from partial specifications; HPRS, which turns task specifications into shaped rewards; an algorithm for safe policy improvement in constrained Markov decision processes; and TD-Magic, which converts pictures of timing diagrams into formal specifications.

title: Unit XIII
summary: Our next autonomous race car, built on the 1:8 Serpent SRX8GTE R electric GT chassis with four-wheel drive.
body: Unit XIII is the next car in our fleet. It is built on the Serpent SRX8GTE R (SER600074), a 1:8 electric GT chassis with four-wheel drive.

The drive pairs a Hobbywing Xerun 4268SD G3 2400 KV motor with a VESC 6 Mk6 HP controller. The planned sensors are a RoboSense Airy LiDAR, a MicroStrain IMU and a ground-facing Holybro H-Flow. For onboard compute, an ASUS NUC 15 Pro and an NVIDIA Jetson are being compared.
RoboRacer Arena covers the simulation side: it turns validated track maps into Isaac Sim environments for training and testing.

title: RoboRacer Arena
imageCaption: Pipeline diagram: track input, environment generation, policy training in Isaac Sim and tests on the physical track
summary: A pipeline that turns track requirements into validated maps and Isaac Sim environments for training and testing racing policies.
body: Learning-based racing needs many training tracks, but each new track needs geometric design, validation and simulation assets. This makes track geometry hard to vary in experiments.

RoboRacer Arena starts from natural-language requirements, generates closed-loop layouts, validates the occupancy maps and builds the matching Isaac Sim environments. It also accepts recorded maps and scaled circuits, giving a first collection of 130 tracks. Eight benchmark maps were converted into simulation assets in under 2.5 seconds each.
We rebuilt our RoboRacer car as a CAD and USD asset. On the physical car, policies trained in the Arena completed ten consecutive laps at commanded speeds up to four times the training speed.

title: Latent Imagination
summary: Model-based reinforcement learning that trains a LiDAR racing policy in simulation and transfers it zero-shot to a real F1TENTH car.
body: World models let reinforcement learning agents learn behavior in a latent imagination space, which makes training more sample-efficient. Their use in real-world robotics had received little study.

We set up time-lap tasks for an F1TENTH racing car with a LiDAR sensor, on test tracks of increasing complexity. Agents that learn in imagination outperformed model-free agents in performance, sample efficiency, task completion and generalization. Generalization depended strongly on the choice of observation model, and world models with long enough memory transferred from simulation to the real car without further training. The paper appeared at ICRA 2022.

title: Learning from Human Attention
summary: Predicting where a human driver looks and using that attention map as an extra input for robot learning.
body: Learning from complex camera images is slow and can fail on unfamiliar data. Humans handle such scenes by focusing on a few points of interest.

We trained a model that predicts human attention from gaze recordings of real-world manual driving, and passed its output as an extra feature map to two tasks: object detection and imitation learning. With predicted attention, the models handled out-of-distribution samples better and learned faster when little data was available.

Three master's theses apply the idea to driving agents, dynamic object detection and autonomous racing. In the racing thesis, attention-based input selection gave faster lap times than a full-image controller.

title: Depth Matters
summary: Adding depth to camera images to steer small-scale autonomous cars, with lightweight models that run on the car.
body: Agents that steer from camera images alone need efficient models that keep working under noise and changing conditions.

We collected data on a small-scale autonomous car driven by an expert with a physical steering wheel, and trained lightweight recurrent controllers on fused RGB and depth input. Depth improved steering prediction over RGB alone. On the real car, the models avoided static and dynamic obstacles under out-of-distribution conditions, and early fusion of depth kept the controller working with frame drops and added noise.
A follow-up workshop paper trains liquid and gated recurrent networks on indoor small-scale driving data and tests them in an outdoor full-scale environment.

title: Learning-Based MPC
summary: Neural approximations of nonlinear MPC that are trained without expert data and checked by a safety filter.
body: Nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) solves an optimization problem at every step, which is costly in real time. Neural approximations are cheaper but usually need many expert NMPC solutions.

Seq-AMPC is a recurrent policy trained through the known dynamics without expert labels; a safety filter with a feasible backup plan checks each proposal. On four benchmarks, including a vehicle and a quadcopter, training took 0.2 to 1.7 GPU hours, 97.2 to 99.1% of proposals were applied, and closed-loop cost stayed within 0.3% of NMPC.
imageCaption: Closed-loop trajectories for four benchmarks: robot arm, vehicle, quadcopter and chain of masses

title: Adaptive Recurrent Control
summary: Fine-tuning pretrained driving policies online, at every time step, with real-time recurrent reinforcement learning.
body: Pretrained driving policies lose performance when conditions at deployment differ from training, for example through changed dynamics or sensor drift.

We fine-tune pretrained policies online with Real-Time Recurrent Reinforcement Learning (RTRRL), a memory-efficient algorithm that updates the policy at every time step without backpropagation through time. We extended RTRRL to LrcSSM, a nonlinear diagonal state-space model, and combined offline behavioral cloning with online fine-tuning. The approach was tested in the CarRacing simulation and on a RoboRacer car with an event camera during real-world line following. LrcSSM-based policies improved fastest and most consistently.
imageCaption: Diagram of offline pre-training and real-time online fine-tuning, next to a RoboRacer car

title: Learning Adaptive Safety
summary: Learning control barrier function parameters together with the policy, to keep multi-robot systems and racing agents safe.
body: Safety in multi-agent systems is hard because little is known about the other agents. Control barrier functions (CBFs) can enforce safety, but current methods make strong assumptions about other agents and need manual tuning.

We showed that the CBF configuration strongly changes the emergent behavior. ASRL is an adaptive safe reinforcement learning framework that learns both the policy and the CBF coefficients by interacting with other agents, keeping cost violations below a set limit. It was evaluated in a multi-robot system and in competitive multi-agent racing, against learning-based and control-theoretic approaches. The paper appeared at ICRA 2024.
imageCaption: Diagram of racing cars whose observations feed a learned policy and a CBF safety filter

title: Multi-Agent Driving Curricula
summary: MATS-Gym, a framework that generates multi-agent traffic scenarios and training curricula for autonomous driving in CARLA.
body: Training driving policies needs many different traffic scenarios, but building scenarios with several heterogeneous agents by hand is slow, especially in detailed simulators.

MATS-Gym uses partial scenario specifications to generate traffic scenarios with a variable number of agents and runs them in the CARLA simulator. It connects scenario engines such as Scenic and ScenarioRunner with multi-agent training frameworks and models the interaction as a partially observable stochastic game. We combined it with unsupervised environment design to generate adaptive curricula, the first use of these algorithms in autonomous driving. The paper appeared at ICRA 2025 and is part of the ADEX project.
imageCaption: Simulated city intersection with the trained car and surrounding traffic highlighted

title: HPRS
summary: HPRS turns safety, target and comfort requirements into a shaped reward for reinforcement learning.
body: Reinforcement learning follows its reward signal, so the reward should match the designer's requirements. Existing automatic methods struggle to produce rewards that train well and satisfy several different requirements at once.

HPRS treats a task as a partially ordered set of safety, target and comfort requirements and turns them into a sum of rewards that respects this order. Its potential-based form makes sparse rewards dense while keeping the optimal policy unchanged. On eight robotics benchmarks, HPRS produced policies that met the requirements, converged faster than the state of the art and needed no manual parameter tuning.
imageCaption: Small race cars on an indoor track bounded by inflatable tubes, with an inset map of the track layout

title: MMDVS-LF
summary: A dataset of event-camera, eye-tracking, RGB, odometry and IMU recordings from people driving a small car along a line.
body: Dynamic vision sensors (DVS) record asynchronous events with high temporal resolution, which suits control tasks, but they are still rarely used in machine learning.

MMDVS-LF is a dataset recorded on a small-scale standardized vehicle during line following. It is the first to combine DVS recordings with eye-tracking data of the drivers. It also contains RGB video, odometry, IMU data and driver demographics. The dataset is meant to support the development of event-based deep learning algorithms.

title: Liquid Neural Networks
summary: Bio-inspired recurrent models, from liquid time-constant networks to liquid-capacitance networks and fast liquid state-space models.
body: Recurrent networks for control should be compact and interpretable and still model complex dynamics. This line of work studies models inspired by biological neurons.

Liquid time-constant networks (LTCs) are continuous-time networks whose time constants vary with the hidden state; they show stable and bounded behavior. Liquid-resistance liquid-capacitance networks (LRCs) dampen the oscillations of LTCs and improve accuracy, tested on time-series benchmarks and an autonomous lane-keeping task. LrcSSM makes such a nonlinear model as fast to compute in parallel as linear state-space layers and outperformed Transformers, LRU, S5 and Mamba on long-range forecasting.
LrcSSM and liquid models are also used in our adaptive-control and domain-shift driving studies.
imageCaption: Two dashcam frames of a road, at sunset and at night, with a predicted steering path drawn in blue

title: NimbleAI
summary: A Horizon Europe project designing 3D-integrated neuromorphic chips that sense and process visual data at the endpoint.
body: Running computer vision on small endpoint chips is limited by energy, latency and silicon area.

NimbleAI takes ideas from biological eyes and brains and from 3D-stacked silicon to build a combined sensing-processing neuromorphic architecture. It senses only data with high information value and discards data once it is not useful. The project targets 100x performance per mW and 50x lower latency than CPU/GPU processing of frame-based video, power in the order of tens of mW and about 50 mm² of silicon. TU Wien (Felix Resch, Radu Grosu) is a partner; the project ran from October 2022 to March 2026.
